extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in probability theory / stochastic processes and PDEs
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook chapter material on multidimensional Brownian motion used to solve boundary-value problems (Dirichlet and Schrödinger equations): definitions (regular boundary point), exit distributions/Poisson kernels, potential kernels/Green's functions, probabilistic representations of PDE solutions, and measure-theoretic foundations for extending measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular point of boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: A point y ∈ ∂G is said to be a regular point if Py(τ = 0) = 1, where τ = inf{t > 0 : Bt ∉ G}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the probabilistic notion of boundary regularity: starting at y the Brownian motion immediately exits G with probability 1. Regularity is used to guarantee boundary continuity of harmonic/solution functions. (See Theorem 9.5.7 and cone condition Theorem 9.5.10 for sufficient conditions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary continuity at regular points (Theorem 9.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded and continuous and y is a regular point of ∂G, then for any sequence xn ∈ G with xn → y we have v(xn) → f(y), where v is the harmonic extension defined by exit expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the criterion that solutions of the Dirichlet problem attain the boundary values at regular points. Proof relies on lower semicontinuity of hitting probabilities and Lemma 9.5.9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower semicontinuity of hitting-time probabilities (Lemma 9.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed t > 0 the map x ↦ Px(τ ≤ t) is lower semicontinuous; i.e., if xn → x then lim inf_n Pxn(τ ≤ t) ≥ Px(τ ≤ t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the Markov property, heat kernel representation, dominated convergence, and monotone limits. This property is used to pass boundary regularity from y to nearby interior points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization of exit to small boundary neighborhood (Lemma 9.5.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If y is regular for G and xn → y, then for every δ > 0 we have Pxn(τ < ∞, Bτ ∈ D(y, δ)) → 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines lower semicontinuity of Px(τ ≤ t) with continuity of Brownian paths and small-time control to show the exit point concentrates near y for starting points approaching a regular boundary point. Used to prove boundary continuity of solution values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone condition for regularity (Theorem 9.5.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists a cone V with vertex y and r > 0 such that V ∩ D(y, r) ⊂ G^c (the exterior), then y is a regular point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A geometric sufficient condition for regularity: existence of a nontrivial cone of exterior points near y guarantees immediate exit when started at y. Proof uses spherical symmetry of the Gaussian and Blumenthal's zero-one law. This is a practical check for boundary regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half-space Poisson kernel and harmonicity (h_θ) (Lemma 9.5.11 & Theorem 9.5.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define h_θ(x,y) = C_d y / (|x − θ|^2 + y^2)^{d/2} for H = {yd > 0}. Then Δ h_θ = 0 in H and for bounded continuous boundary data f the integral u(x,y) = ∫_{R^{d−1}} h_θ(x,y) f(θ,0) dθ solves the Dirichlet problem in H and gives the density of exit distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cd is chosen so ∫ h_θ(0,1) dθ = 1. The kernel is harmonic in the half-space and yields the exit location density Px(B_{τ_H} = (θ,0)). The result includes calculation of derivatives and verification of Δu = 0 and boundary behavior via scaling and dominated convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson kernel for the ball (ky) and boundary integral representation (Theorem 9.5.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: For D = {x : |x| < 1} define k_y(x) = (1 − |x|^2) / |x − y|^d (y on ∂D). If f is bounded and continuous then u(x) = E_x f(B_τ) = ∫_{∂D} k_y(x) f(y) π(dy), where π is normalized surface measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ky(x) is harmonic in x for fixed y and the integral gives the unique bounded harmonic function in the ball with boundary value f. The proof mirrors the half-space case: show Δu = 0 and verify boundary normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exit distribution in two dimensions: Cauchy law
rubrics_metrics.description: When d = 2, the half-space Poisson kernel reduces to h_θ(0,y) = y / π(|θ|^2 + y^2), i.e., a Cauchy density. This corresponds to projection at the stopping time Ty for hitting a given vertical level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: starting at (0,0), the distribution of the horizontal coordinate at the first time the vertical coordinate equals y is a Cauchy law; this follows from scaling and symmetry properties of Brownian motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential kernel G(x,y) and dimensional dichotomy (definitions and formulas) (9.6.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define G(x,y) = ∫_0^∞ p_t(x,y) dt. For d ≥ 3 the integral is finite for x ≠ y and G(x,y) = const·|x − y|^{2−d}. For recurrent cases (d ≤ 2) modify G(x,y) = ∫_0^∞ (p_t(x,y) − a_t) dt with appropriate choices of a_t; this yields G(x,y) = −(1/π) log|x − y| (d=2) and G(x,y) = −|x − y| (d=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The potential kernel is the expected occupation density (integrated heat kernel). The constants/choices of a_t are chosen to make the integral converge and to ensure (1/2)Δ G(·,0) = −δ_0 in the distributional sense. Explicit forms connect G to fundamental harmonic functions φ(|x−y|).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation-time / recurrence vs transience criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a ball D = B(0,r): E_x ∫_0^∞ 1_D(B_t) dt = ∞ when d ≤ 2, while it is finite when d ≥ 3 (so Brownian motion is recurrent in d ≤ 2 and transient in d ≥ 3 for occupation of bounded sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses asymptotics of p_t(x,y) ∼ (2π t)^{-d/2} as t→∞ and Fubini/Tonelli to exchange integrals. This criterion determines whether potential kernels without subtraction converge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic representation and uniqueness for Poisson's equation (Theorems 9.7.1 and 9.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider 1/2 Δ u = −g in bounded G with u = 0 on ∂G and g bounded continuous. Then M_t = u(B_t) + ∫_0^t g(B_s) ds is a local martingale on [0,τ), and any bounded solution u must equal v(x) = E_x ∫_0^τ g(B_t) dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the Feynman–Kac-type representation for the Poisson problem and a uniqueness criterion under boundedness and integrability of τ (Ex τ < ∞). Use dominated convergence to pass limits at τ and boundedness to justify expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient smoothness for solution (Theorem 9.7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If g is Hölder continuous (and defined on R^d with compact support) then the potential w(x) = E_x ∫_0^∞ g(B_t) dt is C^2 when d ≥ 2; in d = 1 it suffices that g is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under these regularity assumptions, w is sufficiently smooth so that v(x) = w(x) − E_x w(B_τ) lies in C^2 and hence the probabilistic representation yields a classical solution. The compact support assumption simplifies integrability and convolution-type formulae (e.g. w(x)=C_d ∫ |x−y|^{2−d} g(y) dy in d≥3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary continuity for Poisson problem at regular points (Theorem 9.7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G and g are bounded and y ∈ ∂G is regular, then for xn ∈ G with xn → y we have v(xn) → 0 (for the homogeneous boundary condition u=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relies on (i) small-time hitting probability tending to 1 for starting points approaching a regular boundary point, and (ii) uniform boundedness of v via Ex τ and boundedness of g. This is the PDE boundary value attainment criterion in probabilistic terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green's function for killed Brownian motion in half-space (Theorem 9.7.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For x ∈ H and nonnegative compactly supported f with support in H, E_x ∫_0^τ f(B_t) dt = ∫_H G(x,y) f(y) dy − ∫_H G(x, ȳ) f(y) dy, where ȳ is reflection of y across the boundary and G is the potential kernel; define G_H(x,y) = G(x,y) − G(x, ȳ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets G_H as expected occupation-time density for Brownian motion killed on leaving H. The reflection principle and Fubini/Tonelli justify the representation; in d=1 GH(x,y)=2(x∧y) explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green's function for ball and inversion formula (Theorems 9.7.7 & 9.7.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the ball D, the Green's function G_D(x,y) = G(x,y) − ∫ [(1−|x|^2)/|x−z|^d] G(z,y) π(dz). In d ≥ 3 this simplifies to G_D(x,y) = G(x,y) − |y|^{2−d} G(x, y/|y|^2), i.e., subtraction of the image under inversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an explicit formula for the Green's function inside the ball by adding an image term to force the boundary condition. Uses harmonicity and inversion mapping y ↦ y/|y|^2. There are analogous log-formulae in d=2 and piecewise linear formulas in d=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale for Schrödinger-type equation (Theorem 9.8.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u satisfies 1/2 Δ u + c u = 0 in G, then M_t = u(B_t) exp(∫_0^t c(B_s) ds) is a local martingale on [0,τ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic Feynman–Kac martingale for the Schrödinger (or killed/weighted) operator. Proof uses Ito's formula and cancellation from the PDE. It is the starting point for probabilistic representation of solutions when exponential weights are integrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness / explosion criterion for Feynman–Kac expectation w(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define w(x) = E_x exp(∫_0^τ c(B_s) ds). Key facts: (i) small-volume exit sets H with |H| ≤ μ satisfy E_x exp(θ τ_H) ≤ 2 for some μ>0 (Lemma 9.8.3); (ii) local comparison: if D(x,2δ) ⊂ G and y ∈ D(x,δ) then w(y) ≤ 2^{d+2} w(x) (Lemma 9.8.4); (iii) if w ≠ ∞ somewhere in connected G then w(x) < ∞ for all x (Theorem 9.8.5); (iv) if |G| < ∞ then sup_x w(x) < ∞ (Theorem 9.8.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria tell when the exponential Feynman–Kac expectation is finite (so probabilistic representation is meaningful). If w ≡ ∞ then there may be no bounded solution of the Schrödinger boundary-value problem. Practical usage: check local small-set exponential moments and propagate finiteness across G.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for Schrödinger boundary problem results (A1–A3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (A1) G is a bounded connected open set. (A2) f and c are bounded and continuous. (A3) w(x) = E_x exp(∫_0^τ c(B_s) ds) is not identically ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three hypotheses are used throughout the Schrödinger-section theorems (uniqueness, boundary attainment, smoothness). Each assumption is essential: boundedness/connectivity for global arguments, bounded continuous coefficients for martingale and dominated convergence, and w < ∞ somewhere to avoid explosion pathology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness representation for Schrödinger PDE (Theorem 9.8.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under (A1)–(A3), any bounded solution u of 1/2 Δ u + c u = 0 in G with boundary f must be v(x) = E_x( f(B_τ) exp(∫_0^τ c(B_s) ds) ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the martingale M_t = u(B_t) exp(∫_0^t c(B_s) ds), dominated convergence, and the finiteness of w to pass limits as t→∞. This is the Feynman–Kac representation and gives uniqueness among bounded solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and boundary attainment for Schrödinger PDE (Theorems 9.8.8–9.8.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the candidate v lies in C^2 then it satisfies 1/2 Δ v + c v = 0 (local Taylor/expectation argument). At regular boundary points y, v(xn) → f(y) for xn→y. If c is Hölder continuous (and (A1)–(A3) hold) then v ∈ C^2 and hence is a classical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine local exit-time Taylor expansions with martingale identities. Hölder continuity of c supplies the necessary regularity to justify interchange of derivatives and integrals and to apply classical PDE regularity results to obtain C^2 smoothness.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-dimensional spectral threshold example (Theorem 9.8.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For d = 1, G = (−a,a), c ≡ γ > 0 and f ≡ 1: E_x e^{γ τ} is finite (and the representation holds) iff 0 < γ < π^2 / (8 a^2); if γ ≥ π^2 / (8 a^2) then E_x e^{γ τ} ≡ ∞ (explosion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit example shows a sharp threshold (related to principal Dirichlet eigenvalue) for the finiteness of the exponential weight and hence for existence of bounded solutions: large positive potentials c can cause the Feynman–Kac expectation to blow up, invalidating probabilistic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carathéodory / extension of measure from semialgebra/algebra (Theorem A.1.1 & A.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a semialgebra and μ defined on S satisfies finite additivity for finite disjoint unions and countable subadditivity in the stated sense, then μ extends uniquely to the algebra generated by S; if the extension is σ-finite it extends uniquely to σ(S). For an algebra A a σ-finite measure μ has a unique extension to σ(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the measure-theoretic foundation used to construct measures from simple collections of sets (e.g. rectangles). The proof proceeds by defining μ on the algebra, constructing outer measure μ*, proving Carathéodory measurability, and invoking uniqueness arguments via the π–λ theorem under σ-finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: π–λ theorem for uniqueness (Theorem A.1.4 & A.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is a π-system and L is a λ-system with P ⊂ L then σ(P) ⊂ L. As consequence: if two measures agree on a π-system and there is an increasing sequence An ∈ P with An ↑ Ω and finite measure, then the measures agree on σ(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem is used to prove uniqueness of measure extensions: verify equality on a generating π-system then conclude equality on the generated σ-field, under a finiteness (σ-finite) condition. The proof constructs the smallest λ-system containing P and shows it is a σ-field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outer measure and Carathéodory measurable sets construction (μ* and measurability condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given μ on an algebra A define μ*(E) = inf Σ μ(A_i) over countable covers E ⊂ ∪ A_i (A_i ∈ A). A set E is Carathéodory-measurable if for all F ⊂ Ω one has μ*(F) = μ*(F ∩ E) + μ*(F ∩ E^c). The family A* of measurable sets is a σ-field and μ* restricted to A* is a measure extending μ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard Carathéodory construction: μ* is an outer measure (monotone, subadditive), all sets in the original algebra are measurable, and the measurable sets form a σ-field on which μ* is countably additive. This yields existence of an extension (not necessarily unique without σ-finiteness).
